title: Low-\(n\) Boolean algebra conjecture
formal: For every integer n≥1, does every countable Boolean algebra with a low-n presentation have a computable presentation?
definitions: For a set X, its jump X′ is the halting set {e: the e-th oracle program with oracle X halts on input e}, for a fixed effective enumeration of programs. Define X^(0)=X and X^(k+1)=(X^(k))′. Low-n means X^(n) is Turing equivalent to the n-th jump of the empty set. A Boolean algebra is a bounded distributive lattice (B,∧,∨,¬,0,1) with b∧¬b=0 and b∨¬b=1. A presentation of an infinite countable algebra has domain N and these operations and constants; a finite presentation has domain {0,…,m−1}. Its atomic diagram is the subset of N coding all true atomic and negated atomic sentences with named domain elements, using a fixed computable syntax encoding. A presentation is computable when this set is decidable. Low-n refers to the atomic diagram. The target asserts existence of a computable copy isomorphic as a Boolean algebra; it does not require a computable isomorphism from the given presentation or a uniform transformation of presentations.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its negation, with exactly the structures and quantifiers specified here. A counterexample must specify some finite n and an algebra with a low-n presentation but no computable copy.
context: The known positive results cover n≤4. The obstruction to extending the method concerns presentations and isomorphisms, not merely the number of jumps in a formula.
why: This tests whether a weak noncomputable presentation of an algebra can always be replaced by a computable one.

import_provenance.original_statement: For every finite n, does any countable Boolean algebra having a low_n presentation also have a computable presentation? Here low_n means that the n-th Turing jump of its atomic diagram is equivalent to the n-th jump of the computable sets; Knight and Stob established the result through n=4.

sentences: A presentation assigns natural-number names to elements of a Boolean algebra.
Its atomic diagram records all basic operations and relations.
Low-n means the nth jump of that diagram adds no power beyond the nth ordinary jump.
The question asks for a computable copy, without a computable isomorphism requirement.
The cited positive cases through n=4 leave the all-finite-n assertion stronger.
